parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a dispatcher. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start until you finish?
I don't know.
When you first sit down at your desk to start work, what is the very first thing you do?
I don't know.
What kind of drone operations do you dispatch?

I dispatch deliveries and inspections. Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, while inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where they started.
Where do these delivery and inspection requests come from, and how do they reach you?
I don't know.
Once you have a delivery or inspection to set up, who do you interact with to make it happen?
I don't know.
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what happened?
I don't know.
When you are getting a delivery or inspection ready, what do you check by hand because you don't trust the system to get it right?

I am responsible for planning and running flights, and I decide which drone flies along which way before signing off a flight. Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility, and our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. However, I do want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.
What are you most worried that a new software service might do wrong?

I worry about the service running on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and that occasionally crashes. We accept a few minutes of interruption, but these system crashes and restarts happen while our operations are active.
When something goes wrong with a flight, what do you need to know right away?
I don't know.
Could you tell me about a time when a flight had a problem, and what you did?
I don't know.
Once you sign off on a flight, who do you hand it over to?
I don't know.
Who else do you communicate with while running a flight?
I don't know.
If a drone loses connection or encounters an emergency, what information do you look for?
I don't know.
How do you work with fleet technicians or the airspace desk?
I don't know.
